title: Operation Income Illusion cracks down on illusory income claims
summary: FTC announcement of coordinated actions against work-at-home, coaching, and trading programs that promised income most buyers never saw.

assertions.quote: Deceptive income claims may be an illusion, but there’s nothing illusory about law enforcers’ commitment to challenge misleading money-making promises.
the vast majority didn’t make anything even approaching the advertised earnings while many made nothing at all
many people lost money, ending up in an even deeper financial hole by taking out loans and racking up credit card debt
deceptive claims that people would make consistent profits and beat the market

verdicts.note: No education program can deliver consistent market-beating returns; regulators have won such cases.

Day trading for a living is shown to be virtually impossible, contrary to what brokerage specialists and course providers often claim; the finding falsifies the promise without establishing intent to deceive.

assertions.quote: you need solid proof to back up your earnings representations before you convey those claims to consumers

verdicts.note: US law requires substantiation of earnings claims.

The FTC Business Opportunity Rule bars earnings claims unless the seller has a reasonable basis, written substantiation, and gives prospects an earnings claim statement with the number and percentage of purchasers who achieved that level; a US legal requirement.

assertions.quote: promoters shouldn’t exploit consumers’ current financial hardship by targeting them with allegedly bogus money-making representations

verdicts.note: Complaint data show spikes in income-scam reports during downturns.

56% of participants earned under $35,000 when they joined and 14% had been in significant debt, 9% had lost a job and 13% had moved in the prior six months, but 42% reported no negative life event; shows low-income recruits, not deliberate targeting.
